content: The clinically significant mean difference (MD) is greater than or equal to 1. However, the upper boundary of the 95% confidence interval (CI) crosses the threshold for what may be considered a meaningful benefit (-1). The use of stimulation was not reported in the study by Weiß (2013, ID: 1153). One trial was excluded from the meta-analysis because it reported within-group change scores. For example, the study by De Castro Moura (2019, ID: 32) included 111 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. No significant within-group changes were observed for either the French auricular acupuncture group or the comparison group, and no statistical comparisons were made between the groups. Regarding inconsistency, no downgrading was applied as most trials showed results in the same direction, indicating a reduction in functional limitation. In another case of inconsistency, a single downgrade was applied. While the results were generally in the same direction, one point estimate was much larger in magnitude, and the confidence intervals of other studies did not overlap with it (I² = 99%). This could not be explained by small subgroup sizes and may indicate substantial heterogeneity. Imprecision was downgraded twice due to small sample sizes and a limited number of events. Another instance of inconsistency led to a single downgrade. The point estimates varied with minimal overlap in confidence intervals (I² = 98%). This could not be attributed to small subgroups and may represent significant heterogeneity. In another case, inconsistency was downgraded once. Most point estimates were in the same direction (I² = 94%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroup sizes and may indicate substantial variability. One trial was excluded from the meta-analysis because it reported within-group change scores. For example, the study by Witt (2006, ID: 2010) included 3093 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. The results significantly favored acupuncture (p < 0.001). The use of stimulation was not reported in the study by Witt (2006, ID: 2010). In the study by Brinkhaus (2006), participants did not report leg pain. The study was conducted in a highto upper-middle-income country and involved mixed acupuncture types (traditional Chinese medicine and dry needling) with manual stimulation. The study by Sung (2020) involved acupuncture with threading stimulation and was rated as having an overall unclear risk of bias. One trial was excluded from the meta-analysis because it reported within-group change scores. For example, the study by Witt (2006, ID: 2010) included 3093 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. The results significantly favored acupuncture (p < 0.001). Another trial was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. The study by Molsberger (2002, ID: 2007) included 186 participants and was rated as having an overall high risk of bias. The authors reported no significant adverse events or side effects in any group. Minor adverse events were reported in several studies. For example, Kerr (2003) noted increased tenderness and leg pain for a few days following treatment. Ushinohama (2016) reported dizziness in one participant, though the treatment group allocation was unknown. Yuan (2016) described transient worsening of back pain (lasting up to one week), acupuncture point pain and bruising, back and leg numbness, discomfort, shoulder pain, and foot pain. Inconsistency was downgraded once in another analysis. The point estimates varied and had overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 41%). This could not be explained by small subgroup sizes and may represent moderate heterogeneity. Imprecision was downgraded twice due to small sample sizes and a limited number of events. Minor adverse events were reported in other studies. For example, Ushinohama (2016) noted dizziness in one participant, and Yuan (2016) described transient worsening of back pain, acupuncture point pain and bruising, back and leg numbness, discomfort, shoulder pain, and foot pain. Inconsistency was not downgraded in one analysis, as the point estimates were in the same direction with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 0%). Minor adverse events were also reported by Kerr (2003), who noted increased tenderness and leg pain for a few days following treatment. In another analysis, inconsistency was downgraded once. The point estimates varied in different directions, with some overlap in confidence intervals (I² = 71%). This could not be explained by small subgroup sizes and may represent substantial heterogeneity. Minor adverse events were reported in other studies. For example, Ushinohama (2016) noted dizziness in one participant, and Yuan (2016) described transient worsening of back pain, acupuncture point pain and bruising, back and leg numbness, discomfort, shoulder pain, and foot pain. The study by Meng (2003) did not specify the range of the pain scale used, though it was assumed to be 0–10. Participants in the study by Meng (2003) did not report leg pain. The study was conducted in a highto upper-middle-income country and involved traditional Chinese medicine acupuncture with electrical stimulation. Several studies investigated the effects of acupuncture and related interventions on chronic nonspecific low back pain. These included electroacupuncture, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and combinations of acupuncture with other therapies such as core stability training, sling exercise training, and caudal epidural injections. The studies varied in their methodologies, sample sizes, and reported outcomes, with some showing significant benefits of acupuncture and others reporting no significant differences. Adverse events were generally minor and transient, including increased tenderness, dizziness, and transient worsening of symptoms. Heterogeneity was a common issue across studies, with inconsistency and imprecision frequently leading to downgrades in the quality of evidence.
